parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
The nuclide $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$ (carbon-14) is unstable and undergoes $\beta^-$ decay, emitting a high-energy electron and an antineutrino to form a new nuclide X. The equation for this decay is shown.
$$^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ........\text{X} + ........\text{e}^- + ^{0}_{0}\bar{\nu}$$
Complete the equation.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens inside the nucleus in beta-minus decay - a neutron changes, but the total number of nucleons stays the same. What does that tell you about the top number for X?
Hint 2: Now balance the lower numbers for charge. The proton number must increase by 1 to balance the -1 from the emitted electron, so work out $6$ plus what gives the new proton number.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Keep the nucleon number the same**
In any nuclear decay the total nucleon number $A$ (top number) is conserved. In $\beta^{-}$ decay a neutron becomes a proton inside the nucleus, so one nucleon simply changes type. That means $A$ does not change. So for X: $$A = 14$$

Step 2: **Increase the proton number by one**
The total proton number $Z$ (bottom number, also charge) must also balance. On the left $Z = 6$. On the right you have X plus an electron with $Z = -1$ plus an antineutrino with $Z = 0$. So: $$6 = Z_{X} + (-1) + 0$$ $$Z_{X} = 7$$ This is nitrogen-14: $$^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + ^{0}_{-1}\text{e}^{-} + ^{0}_{0}\bar{\nu}$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State the equation for $\beta^-$ decay in terms of the fundamental particles involved.
hints: Hint 1: Zoom right inside a neutron. A neutron is $udd$ and a proton is $uud$, so focus on which single quark changes flavour to turn the neutron into a proton.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See beta-minus as a quark change**
A neutron ($udd$) becomes a proton ($uud$). Only one quark actually changes - a down quark turns into an up quark, and the extra charge and energy escape as an electron and an antineutrino: $$\text{d} \rightarrow \text{u} + \text{e}^{-} + \bar{\nu}$$ You can also write the full nucleon version: $$udd \rightarrow uud + \text{e}^{-} + \bar{\nu}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Use your equation from (b)(i) to show how charge is conserved in $\beta^-$ decay.
hints: Hint 1: Write down the charge of each particle in your (b)(i) equation in units of $e$: $d$ is $-1/3$, $u$ is $+2/3$, electron is $-1$. Then compare the total on the left with the total on the right.
parts.proper_answer: Left: $-1/3e$. Right: $+2/3e -1e = -1/3e$, so charge is conserved.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Add up charge on both sides**
Use charges in units of elementary charge $e$: $d = -1/3$, $u = +2/3$, $e^{-} = -1$, $\bar{\nu} = 0$. Left side: $$-1/3e$$ Right side: $$+2/3e + (-1e) + 0 = -1/3e$$ Both sides are equal, so total charge is unchanged. That is conservation of charge.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: Neutrinos were first proposed to exist more than 20 years before they were directly detected, in order to explain a particular experimental observation about $\beta$-decay.
parts.text: State an observation about $\beta$-decay that is explained by the existence of neutrinos.

markscheme_points.text: electrons / $\beta$-particles (emitted from the nucleus) have a (continuous) range of / different (kinetic) energies

hints: Hint 1: If only two particles came out of the decay, energy sharing would fix the electron energy to one value. Think about what was actually seen when scientists measured the kinetic energies of many beta particles from the same isotope.
parts.proper_answer: The emitted $\beta$-particles / electrons have a continuous range of kinetic energies.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember the puzzle of the beta spectrum**
Unlike alpha particles which all come out with the same discrete energy, beta particles from an identical source are found with all energies from near zero up to a maximum. This continuous spread of electron energies was the observation that needed explaining.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Suggest how the existence of neutrinos explains the observation in (c)(i).

markscheme_points.text: the (emitted) neutrinos take varying amounts of the (same total) energy (released in the decay)

hints: Hint 1: The total energy released in each decay is fixed, but the electron does not always get all of it. Think about where the missing, variable part of the energy could be going.
parts.proper_answer: The antineutrino / neutrino carries away the remaining variable amount of energy, so total energy is still conserved.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Share the fixed total energy**
Each decay releases the same total amount of energy. If that energy is shared randomly between two light particles, the electron and the antineutrino, then when the antineutrino takes a lot the electron gets little and vice versa. That naturally gives the electron a continuous range of energies while keeping total energy conserved.
